title: Continuous queue orchestration sleuth
content:
Purpose:
Quick experimental log investigating a set of latency tail regressions we saw in canary for continuous coalescing (aka "coalescer") when user mix includes lots of short requests + intermittent large requests. Goal: figure root cause(s) and actionable mitigations that keep unit-cost benefits of continuous coalescing while restoring 99.9/99.99 P99 tail objectives.

Background + why this is different:
- Recent canary (nightly-2025-10-28) showed P99.9 jump from 220ms -> ~760ms under a mixed synthetic workload. Throughput and average latency were fine; only tails broke.
- Existing notes focus on batch-formation knobs. This runbook focuses on scheduler loop jitter, small GC pauses, and flush-path interactions with KV cache prefill / eviction. Hypothesis: short GC/post-sweep pauses (2-12ms) occasionally delay the scheduler's flush tick, allowing an already-initiated flush to block on kernel path (CUDA memcpy or tensor allocation) and amplify into 100s of ms tail. This is subtle because batching metrics (batch_size, waiting_ms) look normal.

Hypotheses to test (ordered):
1) Scheduler-tick jitter + coalescer age edge-case: a request barely misses previous flush window; scheduler tick is delayed by GC or sysproc, so that request gets coalesced longer than intended then gets flushed into a full compute slot and stalls waiting for memory -> high tail.
2) KV-cache eviction + prefill race: when coalescer flush first hits GPU, cache miss for a long context triggers KV prefetch on critical path; prefetch contention interacts with allocator and leads to stall.
3) Priority demotion interplay: urgent short requests demoted incorrectly because urgency decay timer misfires during scheduler jitter.

Test plan / instrumentation:
- Run targeted synthetic workload that mixes 64-token and 1024-token requests at 3:1 ratio. Reuse production-like interarrival patterns (Poisson, lambda tuned).
- Experiment matrix (parallel runs):
  A. scheduler_tick_jitter_ms: {0, 2, 5}  (introduce jitter to scheduler loop)
  B. coalesce_window_ms: {4, 8, 12} (how long we wait for coalescing)
  C. flush_timeout_ms: {30, 80, 200} (max time scheduler will wait before forced flush)
  D. kv_prefetch_async: {false, true}
  E. urgency_decay_ms: {10, 40} (fast/slow urgency decay)
- Each run: 30 min steady-state after 5 min warmup, collect microtraces, perf counters, GC traces, and GPU timelines.

Commands / harness notes:
- Use harness: tools/latency-harness/mixed-length-ycsb.sh (local copy) with envs:
  EXP_ID=queue-sleuth RUN_TIME=1800 SLO=99.9
- Start profilers: ./scripts/start-trace.sh --microtrace --gc --gpu-timeline --scheduler-annotations
- Logs written to gs://redwood-inference-experiments/queue-sleuth/${EXP_ID}/
- Microtrace marker: TRACE_ID recorded in run metadata.

Key metrics captured:
- P50/P95/P99/P99.9 wall-clock per-invocation
- queue_wait_ms (time from request arrival to begin dispatch)
- coalesce_delay_ms (how long each request sat in coalescer)
- scheduler_tick_delay_ms (time between expected tick and actual loop execution)
- gc_pause_ms (from JVM runtime agent)
- gpu_copy_block_ms (time waiting on device memcpy/alloc)
- kv_prefetch_miss_percent
- demotion_count (priority demotions triggered per minute)

Initial observations (runs 2025-11-02):
- Default knobs (no jitter, coalesce_window_ms=8, flush_timeout_ms=80, kv_prefetch_async=true) reproduced tail regression at P99.9 ~ 690ms.
- Microtraces aligned: long-tail invocations consistently show a short scheduler_tick_delay_ms spike (8-14ms) immediately before a long gpu_copy_block_ms (120-340ms).
- GC traces: many small pauses 2-12ms, frequency ~2/min during the run. Correlation: 70% of scheduler_tick_delay spikes coincide within 5ms of a GC pause.
- When kv_prefetch_async=false (i.e., synchronous prefetch on critical path), P99.9 increased slightly vs baseline, but gpu_copy_block_ms contribution decreased by ~25ms median — suggests prefetch async helped but did not eliminate long memcpy stalls.

Interpretation / theory synthesis:
- Root cause chain appears to be: GC pause -> scheduler tick delayed -> coalescer flush starts later than expected but still hits GPU allocation/copy that has less headroom -> wait on device memcpy or allocator -> long tail. The device-copy stalls are magnified because delayed flush often happens when another large request has already reserved GPU bandwidth.
- KV prefetch is a secondary amplifier. Async prefetch moves CPU latency off the critical path but increases concurrency to GPU, raising probability of contention on memcpy/alloc.
- Priority demotion events observed were often consequence (not cause) of delay; i.e., once latency spikes, demotion logic further changes scheduling distribution.

Mitigations tried (and result):
- Add soft scheduler preempt (fast path): if scheduler_tick_delay_ms > 6ms, force an immediate lightweight flush that only includes small requests (<=128 tokens). Result: P99.9 reduced from ~690ms -> ~240ms in small sample runs. Tradeoff: slight drop in coalescing efficiency (~6% more small batches).
- Staggered async prefetch with backpressure token: limit number of concurrent prefetches to 2. Result: tail reduced another ~40ms and gpu_copy_block_ms 95th moved down. Throughput unaffected.
- GC tuning: bumped young gen target and applied incremental GC options on JVM. Reduced gc_pause_ms frequency by ~60%. Tail further improved but still had occasional outliers.
- Increase flush_timeout_ms to 200ms to avoid forced flush during jitter spikes — this helped average coalescing but made worst-case when stall happened worse (one run hit 980ms P99.9). Not acceptable.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
1) Implement lightweight-size-aware emergency flush: if scheduler tick delayed and there are >N tiny requests, flush tiny-first path (code pointer: scheduler/coalesce/fast_flush_v2). Deploy canary flag controlled.
2) Limit concurrent KV prefetches from the coalescer to 2 by default and expose knob. (PR suggested: #498).
3) JVM GC tuning in runtime image: adopt G1 incremental settings used in infra-srv builds; push experimental image to dedicated canary pool.
4) Add scheduler tick timestamp annotations to microtrace for all production traces (small perf cost) to get better correlation in future incidents.

Longer-term / vetted ideas (for roadmap):
- Move KV prefetch off the critical scheduler thread entirely (background prefetch worker that attaches to cohort lists). Requires more refactor but removes prefetch amplification.
- Add admission control token for GPU copy reservations so that delayed flushes are less likely to collide with heavy memcpy windows.
- Explore moving scheduler out of JVM or isolate GC (e.g., native lightweight scheduler) to avoid GC-induced jitter.

Open questions and things to test next:
- Quantify cost tradeoff for emergency small-only flush across 48h runs with production traces (effects on token cost).
- How does this interact with multi-tenant fairness? small-only emergency flush might starve long requests in tenant with spikes. Run tenant-mix experiments.
- Are there similar jitter sources other than GC? (kernel scheduling, cgroups CPU steals). Add host-level oprofile in next run.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Diego: push PR #498 with default prefetch limit = 2, add flag --coalescer-prefetch-limit. (due 2025-11-09)
- Asha: bake image with G1 tuning and run 24h canary in dedicated pool (tag: gc-tuned-2025-11-07).
- Liam: add scheduler-tick timestamps to microtrace and add visualizer in tools/trace-viewer.
- Capture a 1h full trace with host-level perf counters (CPU steal, rq-squeeze).

Appendix: representative microtrace excerpt (annotated timeline):
- t=0ms: request A (short) arrives
- t=3.1ms: request B (short) arrives
- t=4.8ms: expected scheduler tick (missed due to GC)
- t=12.0ms: actual scheduler tick executes (scheduler_tick_delay_ms=7.2ms) -> flush invoked
- t=12-15ms: coalescer constructs batch (size 3), issues KV prefetch async
- t=28ms: GPU memcpy scheduled, but waits 128ms because a large request's copy is in progress -> gpu_copy_block_ms=128ms
- t=156ms: compute starts -> total wall time for request A = 170ms

References / related tickets:
- INFR-2314 (investigate nightly tail regressions)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/498 (prefetch concurrency limit)
- Slack: #serving-runtime thread CKY1234 (incident discussion)

End of log for initial investigation. Will update after follow-up 24h canary and tenant-mix runs.

Informality notes: this is intentionally a compact field notebook, not a polished postmortem. Lots of half-baked hypotheses here; please call out anything that seems off.
